> **What this case shows** — close your eyes and you sway more: the Romberg phenomenon measures how much
> standing balance leans on vision. On foam, where proprioception is already unreliable, vision carries the
> load — so removing it destabilizes. This case demonstrates and certifies that across 50 subjects. Foam
> COP path length with eyes closed and open comes from the **certified** `swayMetrics`; the **certified**
> `pairedTTest` compares them, reproducing **`scipy.stats.ttest_rel`** *and* base R **`t.test`**
> **bit-for-bit**. Eyes-closed sway is **~1.3x** eyes-open (t=7.6, p~9e-10, in 43/50 subjects). With the
> surface (proprioception) and age effects, this **completes the posturographic sensory triad**.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — pair each subject's eyes-open and eyes-closed sway, then `pairedTTest()`.
**Way of thinking** — balance draws on three inputs: somatosensory (foot/ankle), visual, and vestibular,
weighted by the brain and by age. Probe each by removing or challenging it — foam degrades proprioception,
eyes-closed removes vision — and read the sway increase as that input's contribution.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioAnalysis::pairedTTest()`, `PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics()`.
:::

## Proposition

Across 50 subjects, eyes-closed foam-surface COP path length exceeds eyes-open (mean 217 vs 167 cm, ratio
~1.30, in 43/50 subjects); the paired t-test (t=7.57, df=49, p~8.8e-10) reproduces `scipy.stats.ttest_rel`
and base R `t.test(paired=TRUE)` bit-for-bit.

## Question & goal

**The question is the vision effect and the completion of a story: does closing the eyes on foam increase
sway, and does the certified paired test reproduce the reference?** With the surface (proprioception) and
age effects already certified, this fold adds vision — the third input to standing balance.

## Challenge & approach

For each subject we take the eyes-closed and eyes-open foam quiet-standing COP path lengths (from
`swayMetrics`, certified against the Prieto reference in the
[sway-posturography-bds](../sway-posturography-bds/index.qmd) case) and compare them with `pairedTTest`,
checking t and p against `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` and base R.

```
50 subjects: eyes-open vs eyes-closed foam sway (swayMetrics path length, certified)
  mean 167 vs 217 cm   ·   ratio 1.30   (eyes-closed greater in 43/50)
  pairedTTest → t = 7.57, df = 49, p ~ 8.8e-10   vs scipy.stats.ttest_rel & base R → |diff| = 0
```

## Data

**Santos & Duarte (2016) balance dataset (figshare)**: 50 subjects, one eyes-closed and one eyes-open foam
quiet-standing trial each (60 s, force-plate COP at 100 Hz). Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: each subject's foam COP path length from eyes-open to eyes-closed — most lines rise (red = eyes-closed greater, 43/50), the group mean climbing 167→217 cm (t=7.6, p~9e-10). Right: the posturographic sensory triad — the sway ratio when each input is challenged: proprioception (foam/firm, 2.76x, from the foam-firm case), vision (eyes-closed/open, 1.30x, here); with age (r=0.62 with sway), the three inputs to standing balance.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — closing the eyes shifts nearly every subject up. Right — the two sensory
challenges have different magnitudes (removing reliable proprioception matters more than removing vision,
here), and age modulates both.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| mean eyes-open / eyes-closed sway | 167 / 217 cm |
| **eyes-closed / eyes-open ratio** | **~1.30** |
| eyes-closed > eyes-open | **43 / 50** |
| **paired t** (df 49) | **7.57** |
| −log₁₀ p | 9.1 (p ~ 8.8e-10) |
| vs `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` / base R (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) |

The paired test equals both references exactly, and the vision effect is strong. Values trace to
[`artifacts/sway_summary.csv`](artifacts/sway_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`pairedTTest` — certified in the foam-firm case — reproduces the reference here too, on the certified
`swayMetrics`. The transferable takeaway: **standing balance rests on three inputs. Foam degrades
proprioception (sway 2.76x), eyes-closed removes vision (1.30x), and age erodes the capacity to use both
(sway rises with age, r=0.62). Probing each in turn, with certified metrics and tests, turns posturography
into a mechanistic read-out of who is at risk and why.**

## Open questions

- This shows the vision effect on foam, where it is largest; the classic Romberg is on firm ground, where
  healthy adults compensate and the effect is smaller and age-dependent. The BDS's four vision × surface
  conditions across the full cohort support a two-way analysis of how the sensory contributions combine and
  change with age. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Paired t-test | `pairedTTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| Two-sample t-test / correlation | `twoSampleTTest()`, `correlationTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| Posturography sway metrics | `swayMetrics()` | PhysioMoCap |

**Reading the result.**

- **eyes-closed vs eyes-open** — the sway increase is the visual contribution; larger on foam because the
  other cues are already compromised.
- **the triad together** — report the surface, vision, and age effects side by side; a person whose sway
  jumps most when a given cue is removed is most dependent on it.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioAnalysis); library(PhysioMoCap)

eo <- swayMetrics(cop_eyes_open, 100)$path_length   # per subject
ec <- swayMetrics(cop_eyes_closed, 100)$path_length
pairedTTest(ec, eo)   # t, p, df -- reproduces scipy.stats.ttest_rel and base R bit-for-bit
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/sway_summary.csv`](artifacts/sway_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks the paired
t and p, the bit-exact match against scipy and base R, the eyes-closed > eyes-open direction and ratio, and
the honestly noted scope (reuses the certified pairedTTest; inputs from the certified swayMetrics; the
sensory triad).
